claim: A subcortical pathway quickly conveys visual information to the amygdala in animals.
source: Our ability to rapidly detect threats is thought to be subserved by a subcortical pathway that quickly conveys visual information to the amygdala. This neural shortcut has been demonstrated in animals but has rarely been shown in the human brain.
evidence: Supported by citation to established research on animal models

claim: The subcortical pathway to the amygdala has rarely been shown in the human brain.
source: This neural shortcut has been demonstrated in animals but has rarely been shown in the human brain.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature

claim: It remains unclear whether the subcortical pathway might influence neural activity and behavior in humans.
source: Importantly, it remains unclear whether such a pathway might influence neural activity and behavior.
evidence: Statement of gap in knowledge based on literature review

claim: The study analyzed data from 622 participants from the Human Connectome Project.
source: We conducted a multimodal neuroimaging study of 622 participants from the Human Connectome Project.
evidence: Direct statement of sample size and data source

claim: Probabilistic tractography was applied to diffusion-weighted images to reconstruct a subcortical pathway.
source: We applied probabilistic tractography to diffusion-weighted images, reconstructing a subcortical pathway to the amygdala from the superior colliculus via the pulvinar.
evidence: Description of methodology used in the study

claim: A subcortical pathway was reconstructed from the superior colliculus to the amygdala via the pulvinar.
source: We applied probabilistic tractography to diffusion-weighted images, reconstructing a subcortical pathway to the amygdala from the superior colliculus via the pulvinar.
evidence: Result from tractography analysis

claim: There is evidence for a functionally afferent pulvinar-amygdala pathway during face viewing.
source: We then computationally modeled the flow of haemodynamic activity during a face-viewing task and found evidence for a functionally afferent pulvinar-amygdala pathway.
evidence: Result from computational modeling of fMRI data

claim: Individuals with greater fibre density in the pulvinar-amygdala pathway had stronger dynamic coupling.
source: Critically, individuals with greater fibre density in this pathway also had stronger dynamic coupling and enhanced fearful face recognition.
evidence: Result from correlation analysis between structural and functional measures

claim: Individuals with greater fibre density in the pulvinar-amygdala pathway had enhanced fearful face recognition.
source: Critically, individuals with greater fibre density in this pathway also had stronger dynamic coupling and enhanced fearful face recognition.
evidence: Result from correlation analysis between structural measures and behavioral performance

claim: Rodent research uncovered a subcortical pathway to the amygdala that rapidly transmits auditory signals of threat even when the auditory cortex is destroyed.
source: Decades ago, rodent research uncovered a subcortical pathway to the amygdala that rapidly transmits auditory signals of threat even when the auditory cortex is destroyed (Ledoux, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ledoux, 1998

claim: People with a lesioned primary visual cortex can still respond to affective visual stimuli that they cannot consciously see.
source: Since this discovery, researchers have sought an equivalent visual pathway that might explain how it is that people with a lesioned primary visual cortex can still respond to affective visual stimuli that they cannot consciously see (Tamietto et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tamietto et al., 2010

claim: The superior colliculus, pulvinar, and amygdala have been identified as nodes of a human subcortical route to the amygdala that bypasses the cortex.
source: The superior colliculus, pulvinar, and amygdala have been identified as nodes of a human subcortical route to the amygdala that bypasses the cortex (Morris et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Morris et al., 1999

claim: Subcortical areas consistently coactivate in cortically blind patients when they view emotional stimuli.
source: These subcortical areas consistently coactivate in cortically blind patients (Pegna et al., 2005) – as well as in healthy adults (Vuilleumier et al., 2003; Morris et al., 1999) – when they view emotional stimuli, such as angry or fearful faces.
evidence: Supported by citations to Pegna et al., 2005; Vuilleumier et al., 2003; Morris et al., 1999

claim: Subcortical areas consistently coactivate in healthy adults when they view emotional stimuli.
source: These subcortical areas consistently coactivate in cortically blind patients (Pegna et al., 2005) – as well as in healthy adults (Vuilleumier et al., 2003; Morris et al., 1999) – when they view emotional stimuli, such as angry or fearful faces.
evidence: Supported by citations to Vuilleumier et al., 2003; Morris et al., 1999

claim: Magnetoencephalography studies using computational modelling have consistently found evidence for a forward connection between the pulvinar and amygdala.
source: Magnetoencephalography studies using computational modelling have investigated whether the activation of these subcortical nodes is causally related. These studies have consistently found evidence for a forward connection between the pulvinar and amygdala (McFadyen et al., 2017; Garvert et al., 2014; Rudrauf et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to McFadyen et al., 2017; Garvert et al., 2014; Rudrauf et al., 2008

claim: The dynamic causal relationship between the superior colliculus and the pulvinar remains unexplored in the human brain.
source: The dynamic causal relationship between the superior colliculus and the pulvinar, however, remains unexplored in the human brain (Soares et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement of gap in knowledge supported by citation to Soares et al., 2017

claim: The pulvinar has several functional and cytoarchitectural subregions.
source: The pulvinar also has several functional and cytoarchitectural subregions (Barron et al., 2015) and it is unclear how these connect to the superior colliculus and the amygdala and what roles these subregions may play in mediating transmission along the subcortical route (Koller et al., 2018; Pessoa and Adolphs, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barron et al., 2015

claim: It is unclear how pulvinar subregions connect to the superior colliculus and the amygdala.
source: The pulvinar also has several functional and cytoarchitectural subregions (Barron et al., 2015) and it is unclear how these connect to the superior colliculus and the amygdala and what roles these subregions may play in mediating transmission along the subcortical route (Koller et al., 2018; Pessoa and Adolphs, 2010).
evidence: Statement of gap in knowledge supported by citations to Koller et al., 2018; Pessoa and Adolphs, 2010

claim: The hypothesis that the subcortical route rapidly transfers information from the retina to the amygdala without interference has been heavily criticised.
source: As such, the hypothesis that the subcortical route rapidly transfers information from the retina to the amygdala without interference has been heavily criticised (Pessoa and Adolphs, 2010; Pessoa and Adolphs, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pessoa and Adolphs, 2010; Pessoa and Adolphs, 2011

claim: The pulvinar is highly connected with a widespread network of cortical regions that may contribute to transmission along the subcortical route.
source: Furthermore, the pulvinar is highly connected with a widespread network of cortical regions that may contribute to transmission along the subcortical route (Bridge et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bridge et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2016

claim: It remains unknown whether the functional activation of the human superior colliculus, pulvinar and amygdala during affective processing bears any relation to an underlying structural pathway.
source: Hence, it remains unknown whether the functional activation of the human superior colliculus, pulvinar and amygdala during affective processing bears any relation to an underlying structural pathway (Pessoa and Adolphs, 2010).
evidence: Statement of gap in knowledge supported by citation to Pessoa and Adolphs, 2010

claim: Recent animal research has revealed several potential direct subcortical pathways that have a causal relationship with fearful behaviour in response to visual threats.
source: Recent animal research has revealed several potential direct subcortical pathways that have a causal relationship with fearful behaviour in response to visual threats (Zhou et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2015; Shang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2015; Shang et al., 2015

claim: In the absence of relevant postmortem human research, anatomical knowledge of the human subcortical route to the amygdala can only be derived from tractography of diffusion-weighted images.
source: In the absence of relevant postmortem human research, however, our anatomical knowledge of the human subcortical route to the amygdala can only be derived from tractography of diffusion-weighted images (DWI).
evidence: Statement about methodological limitations based on current state of knowledge

claim: Tamietto et al., 2012 examined DWIs from a blindsight patient whose left primary visual cortex was destroyed.
source: Tamietto et al., 2012 examined DWIs from a blindsight patient whose left primary visual cortex was destroyed.
evidence: Description of prior study supported by citation

claim: The subcortical route had greater fractional anisotropy in the patient's damaged hemisphere, suggesting a neuroplastic increase in structural connectivity to compensate for the disrupted cortical pathways.
source: Critically, the subcortical route had greater fractional anisotropy in the patient's damaged hemisphere, suggesting a neuroplastic increase in structural connectivity to compensate for the disrupted cortical pathways (Tamietto et al., 2012).
evidence: Finding from prior study supported by citation to Tamietto et al., 2012

claim: Rafal et al. (2015) used tractography to investigate the subcortical route in 20 healthy humans and eight macaques.
source: In a similar study, Rafal et al. (2015) used tractography to investigate the subcortical route in 20 healthy humans and eight macaques.
evidence: Description of prior study supported by citation

claim: The subcortical route was reconstructed in both hemispheres for 19 of the 20 human participants and 7 of the eight macaques.
source: The subcortical route was reconstructed in both hemispheres for 19 of the 20 human participants and 7 of the eight macaques (Rafal et al., 2015).
evidence: Finding from prior study supported by citation to Rafal et al., 2015

claim: Individuals with greater fractional anisotropy along the subcortical route had a stronger bias toward threat when making saccades to scenes.
source: Notably, this sample of human participants was recently expanded and re-examined, further demonstrating that individuals with greater fractional anisotropy along the subcortical route also had a stronger bias toward threat when making saccades to scenes (Koller et al., 2018).
evidence: Finding from prior study supported by citation to Koller et al., 2018

claim: Diffusion tractography cannot reveal the direction of information transfer.
source: Diffusion tractography may grant insight into the strength of anatomical connectivity between regions, but it cannot reveal the direction of information transfer nor can it be used as direct evidence alone for the anatomical existence of a neural pathway.
evidence: Statement about methodological limitations based on established knowledge

claim: Diffusion tractography cannot be used as direct evidence alone for the anatomical existence of a neural pathway.
source: Diffusion tractography may grant insight into the strength of anatomical connectivity between regions, but it cannot reveal the direction of information transfer nor can it be used as direct evidence alone for the anatomical existence of a neural pathway.
evidence: Statement about methodological limitations based on established knowledge

claim: The anatomical presence and the direction-specific neural flow of emotional visual information along the subcortical route has never been concurrently investigated in humans.
source: The anatomical presence and the direction-specific neural flow of emotional visual information along the subcortical route has never been concurrently investigated in humans to definitively show that the subcortical route is a direct, afferent pathway specifically associated with fear (Pessoa and Adolphs, 2010; Pessoa and Adolphs, 2011).
evidence: Statement of gap in knowledge supported by citations to Pessoa and Adolphs, 2010; Pessoa and Adolphs, 2011

claim: The subcortical pathway has potential for rapid information transfer.
source: Such a finding would have important implications for the very foundation of visual threat perception, given this pathway's potential for rapid information transfer (McFadyen et al., 2017; Silverstein and Ingvar, 2015) and unconscious processing (Tamietto et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to McFadyen et al., 2017; Silverstein and Ingvar, 2015

claim: The subcortical pathway has potential for unconscious processing.
source: Such a finding would have important implications for the very foundation of visual threat perception, given this pathway's potential for rapid information transfer (McFadyen et al., 2017; Silverstein and Ingvar, 2015) and unconscious processing (Tamietto et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tamietto et al., 2010

claim: The superior colliculus was connected to the pulvinar in global tractography analysis.
source: We discovered that the superior colliculus (SC) was connected to the pulvinar (PUL; fibre counts for PUL; left: M = 13.23, SD = 5.56, right: M = 13.00, SD = 5.59, minimum of 2 fibres per participant).
evidence: Result from global tractography analysis with descriptive statistics

claim: The pulvinar and the amygdala were connected in global tractography analysis.
source: The pulvinar and the amygdala were also connected (fibre counts for left: M = 5.33, SD = 2.79, and right: M = 6.75, SD = 2.90), with most participants having at least one connecting fibre (zero fibres for left PUL-AMG for eight participants – only 1.28% of total sample).
evidence: Result from global tractography analysis with descriptive statistics

claim: Global tractography can reliably detect evidence for a subcortical route across a large sample of participants.
source: Thus, this relatively conservative method of fibre reconstruction (as it takes into account the entire brain) can reliably detect evidence for a subcortical route across a large sample of participants.
evidence: Inference drawn from the tractography results

claim: Up to 60% of the subcortical route overlapped with major fasciculi, mainly the anterior thalamic radiation and the corticospinal tract, as well as the inferior longitudinal and fronto-occipital fasciculi.
source: This revealed that up to 60% of the subcortical route overlapped with major fasciculi, mainly the anterior thalamic radiation and the corticospinal tract, as well as the inferior longitudinal and fronto-occipital fasciculi.
evidence: Result from overlap analysis with white matter atlas

claim: For the SC-PUL pathway, the major overlap was found in the anterior thalamic radiation in the left (M = 56.11%, SD = 15.56%, range = 9.46% to 100%) and right (M = 55.78%, SD = 16.97%, range = 4.81% to 96.55%) hemispheres.
source: For the SC-PUL pathway, the major overlap was found in the anterior thalamic radiation in the left (M = 56.11%, SD = 15.56%, range = 9.46% to 100%) and right (M = 55.78%, SD = 16.97%, range = 4.81% to 96.55%) hemispheres, followed by the corticospinal tract (left: M = 4.82%, SD = 6.08%, range = 0% to 33%; right: M = 21.06%, SD = 12.75%, range = 0% to 69.09%; see Figure 1).
evidence: Result from overlap analysis with descriptive statistics and reference to Figure 1

claim: Track density of the PUL-AMG pathway was mostly found in the corticospinal tract (left: M = 33.69%, SD = 18.56%, range = 0% to 88.89%; right: M = 36.73%, SD = 17.80%, range = 0% to 82.35%).
source: Track density of the PUL-AMG pathway was mostly found in the corticospinal tract (left: M = 33.69%, SD = 18.56%, range = 0% to 88.89%; right: M = 36.73%, SD = 17.80%, range = 0% to 82.35%), followed by the anterior thalamic radiation (left: M = 20.58%, SD = 14.10%, range = 0% to 70%; right: M = 11.32%, SD = 8.88%, range = 0% to 52.75%).
evidence: Result from overlap analysis with descriptive statistics

claim: There were significantly more fibres connecting the SC and PUL than the PUL and AMG.
source: After covarying out head motion and removing four participants with outlying standardised residuals (z-score threshold ±3), we established that there were significantly more fibres connecting the SC and PUL (M = 13.119, 95% CI = [12.738, 13.500]) than the PUL and AMG (M = 6.040, 95% CI = [5.867, 6.214]; F(1,616) = 433.286, p=2.842 × 10−73, ηp2 =.413).
evidence: Result from statistical analysis (ANOVA) of global tractography data

claim: There were more reconstructed fibres for the right than the left hemisphere.
source: We also found a hemispheric lateralisation, such that there were more reconstructed fibres for the right (M = 9.879, 95% CI = [9.624, 10.135]) than the left (M = 9.280, 95% CI = [9.023, 9.537]) hemisphere (F(1,616) = 7.583, p=0.006, ηp2 =.012), specifically for the PUL-AMG pathway (F(1,616) = 16.025, p=7.000 × 10−5, ηp2 =.025; t(617) = −9.785, p=4.070 × 10−18, 95% CI [−1.714,–1.141]).
evidence: Result from statistical analysis (ANOVA) of global tractography data

claim: The global tractography fibres between the SC and PUL connected predominantly to the inferior and anterior pulvinar.
source: This masking approach revealed that the global tractography fibres present between the SC and PUL connected predominantly to the inferior and anterior pulvinar (see Appendix 1—tables 3 to 5 for detailed statistics).
evidence: Result from subregion analysis of global tractography data

claim: Between the PUL and AMG, fibres terminated almost exclusively in the inferior PUL and then predominantly in the basolateral AMG.
source: Between the PUL and AMG, fibres terminated almost exclusively in the inferior PUL and then predominantly in the basolateral AMG.
evidence: Result from subregion analysis of global tractography data

claim: The inferior pulvinar served as the connecting node between the SC and the basolateral AMG for the globally reconstructed subcortical pathway.
source: Hence, the inferior pulvinar served as the connecting node between the SC and the basolateral AMG for the globally reconstructed subcortical pathway.
evidence: Inference drawn from subregion analysis results

claim: The number of streamlines from local tractography was significantly different from chance for each connection.
source: We found that the number of streamlines was significantly different from chance for each connection, as determined by a series of paired two-sided t-tests (see Appendix 1—table 9), suggesting that the DWI data produced meaningful streamlines between our ROIs.
evidence: Result from statistical comparison with null distribution

claim: There was greater fibre density for the SC-PUL connection than the PUL-AMG connection in local tractography.
source: The apparent fibre density of the streamlines generated using local tractography followed the same pattern as the global tractography fibre counts, such that there was greater fibre density for the SC-PUL connection (M = 5.793, 95% CI = [5.663, 5.923]) than the PUL-AMG connection (M = 4.461, 95% CI = [4.368, 4.554]; F(1,607) = 69.586, p=4.930 × 10−16, ηp2 =.103), after accounting for head motion and removing 13 outliers according to their residuals.
evidence: Result from statistical analysis (ANOVA) of local tractography data

claim: Fibre density was greater on the right than the left for the PUL-AMG connection in local tractography.
source: Fibre density was also greater on the right (M = 4.935, 95% CI = [4.822, 5.048]) than the left (M = 3.987, 95% CI = [3.889, 4.086]) for the PUL-AMG connection (t(608) = −18.205, p=1.960 × 10−59, 95% CI [−1.050,–0.845]) while, in contrast, there was greater fibre density for the left than right SC-PUL connection (t(608) = 10.749, p=8.600×10−25, 95% CI = [0.742, 1.073]; F(1,607) = 162.475, p=3.828 × 10−33, ηp2 =.211).
evidence: Result from statistical analysis (t-test) of local tractography data

claim: There was greater fibre density for the left than right SC-PUL connection in local tractography.
source: Fibre density was also greater on the right (M = 4.935, 95% CI = [4.822, 5.048]) than the left (M = 3.987, 95% CI = [3.889, 4.086]) for the PUL-AMG connection (t(608) = −18.205, p=1.960 × 10−59, 95% CI [−1.050,–0.845]) while, in contrast, there was greater fibre density for the left than right SC-PUL connection (t(608) = 10.749, p=8.600×10−25, 95% CI = [0.742, 1.073]; F(1,607) = 162.475, p=3.828 × 10−33, ηp2 =.211).
evidence: Result from statistical analysis (t-test) of local tractography data

claim: The tractography analyses provide strong convergent evidence for a subcortical white matter pathway to the amygdala in the human brain.
source: Taken together, our tractography analyses provide strong convergent evidence for a subcortical white matter pathway to the amygdala in the human brain.
evidence: Summary inference drawn from both tractography methods

claim: Participants were most accurate with identifying the emotional expression of happy faces (M = 7.96, SD = 0.21).
source: Participants were most accurate with identifying the emotional expression of happy faces (M = 7.96, SD = 0.21), followed by neutral (M = 7.22, SD = 1.18), and then fearful faces (M = 7.02, SD = 1.03).
evidence: Result from behavioral task with descriptive statistics

claim: Recognition was poorest for angry (M = 6.86, SD = 0.98) and sad faces (M = 6.82, SD = 1.12).
source: Recognition was poorest for angry (M = 6.86, SD = 0.98) and sad faces (M = 6.82, SD = 1.12).
evidence: Result from behavioral task with descriptive statistics

claim: There was a significant relationship between local tractography and recognition accuracy for fearful faces.
source: While there were no significant multivariate relationships between global tractography and emotion recognition (see Appendix 1—tables 10 and 11 for detailed statistics), there was a significant relationship between local tractography and recognition accuracy for fearful faces (F(4,598) = 2.501, p=0.042, Wilk's Λ = 0.984, np2 = 0.016; see Figure 2B).
evidence: Result from multivariate regression analysis with reference to Figure 2B

claim: The relationship between local tractography and fearful face recognition was driven predominantly by fibre density of the left (β = 0.140, p=0.004) and right (β = 0.143, p=0.012) PUL-AMG connections.
source: This was driven predominantly by fibre density of the left (β = 0.140, p=0.004) and right (β = 0.143, p=0.012) PUL-AMG connections' local fibre density.
evidence: Result from multivariate regression analysis showing specific parameter estimates

claim: The fibre density of the PUL-AMG half of the subcortical route is associated with fearful face recognition more so than with other negative (sad) or threatening (angry) emotional expressions.
source: These results suggest that the fibre density of the PUL-AMG half of the subcortical route is associated with fearful face recognition more so than with other negative (sad) or threatening (angry) emotional expressions.
evidence: Inference drawn from multivariate regression results

claim: The faces-vs-shapes fMRI task revealed a network of significant BOLD clusters spread across occipital, temporal, frontal, parietal, and subcortical areas.
source: This revealed a network of significant BOLD clusters spread across occipital, temporal, frontal, parietal, and subcortical areas, replicating previous work with this dataset (Barch et al., 2013).
evidence: Result from whole-brain fMRI analysis, supported by citation to Barch et al., 2013

claim: The most significant cluster included the left and right amygdala as well as the left and right fusiform gyri (FG) and inferior occipital gyri (IOG).
source: Critically, the most significant cluster included the left and right amygdala as well as the left and right fusiform gyri (FG) and inferior occipital gyri (IOG).
evidence: Result from whole-brain fMRI analysis

claim: The fusiform gyrus and inferior occipital gyrus are key nodes in the cortical visual processing stream for faces, which may feed information forward to the amygdala.
source: These latter two regions are key nodes in the cortical visual processing stream for faces, which may feed information forward to the amygdala (Tamietto et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement about functional role supported by citation to Tamietto et al., 2010

claim: Significant voxels were found in the superior colliculus and pulvinar during face viewing (proportion of significant voxels within each mask: left SC = 65.08%, right SC = 73.55%, left PUL = 36.13%, right PUL = 51.49%).
source: This revealed significant voxels in each area (proportion of significant voxels within each mask: left SC = 65.08%, right SC = 73.55%, left PUL = 36.13%, right PUL = 51.49%).
evidence: Result from ROI-based fMRI analysis with descriptive statistics

claim: The winning family was the 'Dual with SC and PUL input' family (expected probability = 67.34%, exceedance probability = 100%).
source: The winning family was the 'Dual with SC and PUL input' family (expected probability = 67.34%, exceedance probability = 100%) and the winning model across the entire model space was also within this family (expected probability = 21.24%, exceedance probability = 98.01%, protected exceedance probability = 98.18%; see Figure 4).
evidence: Result from Bayesian model selection with reference to Figure 4

claim: The winning model included reciprocal cortical connections between IOG and FG and between FG and the amygdala.
source: This model included reciprocal cortical connections between IOG and FG and between FG and the amygdala.
evidence: Description of winning model structure from DCM analysis

claim: The winning model included a forwards-only subcortical route from the superior colliculus to the pulvinar to the amygdala, with input to both the superior colliculus and the pulvinar.
source: It also included a forwards-only subcortical route from the superior colliculus to the pulvinar to the amygdala, with input to both the superior colliculus and the pulvinar.
evidence: Description of winning model structure from DCM analysis

claim: The Bayesian Omnibus Risk score was p=1.78×10−124, indicating a very small chance that the winning model was indistinguishable from all models tested.
source: The Bayesian Omnibus Risk score was p=1.78×10−124, indicating a very small chance that the winning model was indistinguishable from all models tested (Rigoux et al., 2014).
evidence: Result from Bayesian model selection with citation to Rigoux et al., 2014

claim: All connectivity modulations were significant except for the backward connection from left and right FG to left IOG.
source: We removed extreme outliers (>3 SDs from mean) participants from each connection (M = 5.25, range = 3 to 8 participants excluded from sample of 237) and found that all connectivity modulations were significant (one sample t-tests against a test value of 1; see Appendix 1—table 13 for detailed statistics) except for the backward connection from left and right FG to left IOG (see Figure 5).
evidence: Result from statistical analysis (t-tests) of DCM parameters with reference to Figure 5

claim: A subcortical route for processing faces is likely present within the general population.
source: These results suggest that the modulation of these connections by faces was consistently strong and so we can infer that a subcortical route for processing faces is likely present within the general population.
evidence: Inference drawn from DCM parameter estimates

claim: Participants with more global fibres had greater modulatory activity for the right (r = 0.180, p = 0.004, pbonf = 0.032) PUL-AMG connection.
source: After removing multivariate outliers (leaving N = 213; see Appendix 1—table 12 for details), we discovered that participants with more global fibres also had greater modulatory activity for the right (r = 0.180, p = 0.004, pbonf = 0.032; see Figure 6) but not the left (r = 0.095, p = 0.084, pbonf = 0.672) PUL-AMG connection.
evidence: Result from partial correlation analysis with reference to Figure 6

claim: The SC-PUL connection was not significantly related to its corresponding DCM parameters for global or local tractography.
source: The SC-PUL connection was not significantly related to its corresponding DCM parameters for global (left: r = −0.022, p = 0.627, pbonf = 1.000; right: r = 0.002, p = 0.488, pbonf = 1.000) or local (left: r = −0.101, p = 0.928, pbonf = 1.000; right: r = −0.028, p = 0.659, pbonf = 1.000) tractography.
evidence: Result from partial correlation analysis

claim: This study is the first to successfully harmonise functional and structural information about the subcortical pulvinar connection to the amygdala.
source: Thus, our study is the first to successfully harmonise functional and structural information about the subcortical pulvinar connection to the amygdala.
evidence: Summary claim about novelty of the study

claim: This study marks the first time that structural and effective connectivity have been concurrently investigated in one large sample to address the controversy on the existence and functional role of the putative subcortical route to the amygdala.
source: This study marks the first time that structural and effective connectivity have been concurrently investigated in the one large sample to address the controversy on the existence and functional role of the putative subcortical route to the amygdala.
evidence: Summary claim about novelty of the study

claim: Up to 60% of the subcortical route's fibre density overlapped with major fasciculi, including the corticospinal tract, anterior thalamic radiation, inferior longitudinal fasiculus, and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus.
source: Up to 60% of its fibre density overlapped with major fasciculi, including the corticospinal tract, anterior thalamic radiation, inferior longitudinal fasiculus, and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus.
evidence: Result from overlap analysis with white matter atlas

claim: Tractography of diffusion images is susceptible to both false positives and false negatives and thus is seldom used in isolation to determine the existence of particular neuroanatomical pathways.
source: Tractography of diffusion images is susceptible to both false positives and false negatives and thus is seldom used in isolation to determine the existence of particular neuroanatomical pathways (Jbabdi and Johansen-Berg, 2011).
evidence: Statement about methodological limitations supported by citation to Jbabdi and Johansen-Berg, 2011

claim: The validity of the tractographically reconstructed subcortical route was established by directly relating measures of fibre density to both behaviour and effective connectivity, as well as by using two different tractography methods.
source: We established the validity of our tractographically reconstructed subcortical route by directly relating our measures of fibre density to both behaviour and effective connectivity, as well as by using two different tractography methods.
evidence: Description of validation approach used in the study

claim: If the fibre density measures were simply due to noise, theoretically relevant relationships with fearful face processing would not have emerged within this large sample of individuals.
source: Had the fibre density measures been simply due to noise, we would not have expected these theoretically relevant relationships with fearful face processing to emerge within this large sample of individuals.
evidence: Logical inference about the validity of the findings

claim: The intermodal relationships were only found for the pulvinar-amygdala connection, despite there being greater fibre density between the superior colliculus and the pulvinar.
source: Notably, these intermodal relationships were only found for the pulvinar-amygdala connection, despite there being greater fibre density between the superior colliculus and the pulvinar and this connection being present in the winning dynamic causal model.
evidence: Summary of findings comparing different connections

claim: There was relatively less BOLD signal-to-noise ratio in the superior colliculus due to its small size and proximity to major blood vessels in the brain stem.
source: One explanation for this is that we had relatively less BOLD signal-to-noise ratio in the superior colliculus due to its small size and proximity to major blood vessels in the brain stem (Wall et al., 2009), thus weakening the likelihood of finding consistent covariance of its functional coupling with fibre density.
evidence: Explanation for findings supported by citation to Wall et al., 2009

claim: The pulvinar plays a significant functional role in the subcortical route to the amygdala.
source: Another explanation, particularly regarding the behaviour-tractography relationship, is that the pulvinar plays a significant functional role in the subcortical route to the amygdala.
evidence: Inference drawn from the pattern of results

claim: Research on macaques has demonstrated the pulvinar's response to emotional faces.
source: Research on macaques has demonstrated the pulvinar's response to emotional faces (Soares et al., 2017; Maior et al., 2010) and its role in modulating attention (Soares et al., 2017) and so we would indeed expect the strength of the pulvinar-amygdala connection to be more predictive of fearful face recognition.
evidence: Supported by citations to Soares et al., 2017; Maior et al., 2010

claim: Research on macaques has demonstrated the pulvinar's role in modulating attention.
source: Research on macaques has demonstrated the pulvinar's response to emotional faces (Soares et al., 2017; Maior et al., 2010) and its role in modulating attention (Soares et al., 2017) and so we would indeed expect the strength of the pulvinar-amygdala connection to be more predictive of fearful face recognition.
evidence: Supported by citation to Soares et al., 2017

claim: The likelihood of reconstructing a continuous streamline of axon bundles traversing the pulvinar's grey matter may have been restricted by grey-white matter boundary constraints in anatomically-constrained tractography.
source: Given that the pulvinar is made up of thalamic cell bodies (grey matter), the likelihood of reconstructing a continuous streamline of axon bundles traversing the pulvinar's grey matter may have been restricted by these boundary constraints.
evidence: Explanation of methodological limitation based on anatomical knowledge

claim: Previous studies that have not imposed grey-white matter boundary constraints have successfully traced a continuous pathway from the superior colliculus to the amygdala via the pulvinar.
source: Previous studies that have not imposed these constraints have successfully traced a continuous pathway from the superior colliculus to the amygdala via the pulvinar (Rafal et al., 2015; Tamietto et al., 2012), supporting animal research showing that inferior-lateral pulvinar neurons receiving superior colliculus afferents also have efferent connections to the lateral amygdala (Day-Brown et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rafal et al., 2015; Tamietto et al., 2012; Day-Brown et al., 2010

claim: Animal research shows that inferior-lateral pulvinar neurons receiving superior colliculus afferents also have efferent connections to the lateral amygdala.
source: Previous studies that have not imposed these constraints have successfully traced a continuous pathway from the superior colliculus to the amygdala via the pulvinar (Rafal et al., 2015; Tamietto et al., 2012), supporting animal research showing that inferior-lateral pulvinar neurons receiving superior colliculus afferents also have efferent connections to the lateral amygdala (Day-Brown et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Day-Brown et al., 2010

claim: The superior colliculus projects predominantly onto the inferior (and anterior) pulvinar.
source: Our investigation into pulvinar and amygdala subregions support these findings, such that we found the superior colliculus to project predominantly onto the inferior (and anterior) pulvinar, which was the same subregion to receive the vast majority of fibres from the amygdala (see Figure 1).
evidence: Result from subregion analysis with reference to Figure 1

claim: Pulvinar fibres terminated predominantly within the basolateral amygdala, which is known to process visual information about threat and faces.
source: Furthermore, pulvinar fibres terminated predominantly within the basolateral amygdala, which is known to process visual information about threat and faces (Hortensius et al., 2016).
evidence: Result from subregion analysis supported by citation to Hortensius et al., 2016

claim: The continuity of information flow along the subcortical route is a disputed feature due to the strong cortical influences on the pulvinar.
source: While our results suggest that the inferior pulvinar may serve as a disynaptic connection point between the superior colliculus and amygdala, the continuity of information flow along the subcortical route is still a disputed feature due to the strong cortical influences on the pulvinar (Bridge et al., 2016; Pessoa and Adolphs, 2011).
evidence: Statement about ongoing debate supported by citations to Bridge et al., 2016; Pessoa and Adolphs, 2011

claim: Research on blindsight patients has found evidence only for low spatial frequencies which suggests that such information originated from magnocellular cells in the superior colliculus.
source: Research on blindsight patients has found evidence only for low spatial frequencies which suggests that such information originated from magnocellular cells in the superior colliculus (Burra et al., 2017; Méndez-Bértolo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Burra et al., 2017; Méndez-Bértolo et al., 2016

claim: Work in healthy participants has found no spatial frequency preference, which suggests that rapid pulvinar-amygdala transmission might include input from other parvocellular pathways.
source: On the other hand, work in healthy participants has found no such spatial frequency preference, which suggests that rapid pulvinar-amygdala transmission might include input from other parvocellular pathways (McFadyen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to McFadyen et al., 2017

claim: The winning model did not include cortical connections between the pulvinar and the inferior occipital gyrus.
source: The winning effective connectivity model, however, did not include cortical connections between the pulvinar and the inferior occipital gyrus.
evidence: Result from DCM model selection

claim: It is unlikely that the primary visual cortex contributed to the information transmitted along the subcortical route.
source: Hence, it is unlikely that the primary visual cortex contributed (either via direct anatomical connections or functional coupling along the ventral visual stream; Pessoa and Adolphs, 2010) to the information transmitted along the subcortical route.
evidence: Inference drawn from DCM results with citation to Pessoa and Adolphs, 2010

claim: The winning model included input to the superior colliculus as well as directly to the pulvinar.
source: The winning model did, however, include input to the superior colliculus as well as directly to the pulvinar, which could reflect direct retinal input or input from areas not explicitly included in the model, such as the parietal cortex, temporal cortex, or the LGN (Bridge et al., 2016), that may transmit both low and high spatial frequency information.
evidence: Result from DCM with speculation about possible sources supported by citation to Bridge et al., 2016

claim: Greater pulvinar-amygdala fibre density related to better fearful face recognition.
source: While our findings demonstrated that greater pulvinar-amygdala fibre density related to better fearful face recognition, it remains to be seen how this might compare with structural connectivity of other cortical networks.
evidence: Summary of behavioral finding from the study

claim: Evidence from blindsight patients suggests that the subcortical connection strengthens when cortical connections are destroyed.
source: Evidence from blindsight patients suggests that this subcortical connection ensures redundancy and compensation, such that it strengthens when cortical connections are destroyed (Tamietto et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tamietto et al., 2012

claim: Structural connectivity between the superior colliculus, pulvinar, and amygdala is weakened in individuals with autism compared to healthy controls.
source: For example, structural connectivity between the superior colliculus, pulvinar, and amygdala is weakened in individuals with autism compared to healthy controls (Hu et al., 2017), and BOLD signal to fearful faces is reduced in these areas (Kleinhans et al., 2011; Green et al., 2017), unless participants are explicitly instructed to fixate on the eyes (Hadjikhani et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hu et al., 2017; Kleinhans et al., 2011; Green et al., 2017; Hadjikhani et al., 2017

claim: BOLD signal to fearful faces is reduced in the superior colliculus, pulvinar, and amygdala in individuals with autism.
source: For example, structural connectivity between the superior colliculus, pulvinar, and amygdala is weakened in individuals with autism compared to healthy controls (Hu et al., 2017), and BOLD signal to fearful faces is reduced in these areas (Kleinhans et al., 2011; Green et al., 2017), unless participants are explicitly instructed to fixate on the eyes (Hadjikhani et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kleinhans et al., 2011; Green et al., 2017; Hadjikhani et al., 2017

claim: People who suffer from anxiety show hyperactive activity along the subcortical route compared to non-anxious individuals.
source: On the other hand, people who suffer from anxiety show hyperactive activity along the subcortical route compared to non-anxious individuals (Hakamata et al., 2016; Tadayonnejad et al., 2016; Nakataki et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hakamata et al., 2016; Tadayonnejad et al., 2016; Nakataki et al., 2017

claim: Both the local and global tractography showed greater fibre density along the right than the left for the pulvinar-amygdala connection.
source: We observed hemispheric lateralisation of the pulvinar-amygdala connection, such that both the local and global tractography showed greater fibre density along the right than the left, and there were stronger tractography-behaviour and tractography-connectivity relationships for the right than the left.
evidence: Summary of lateralization findings from tractography analyses

claim: There were stronger tractography-behaviour and tractography-connectivity relationships for the right than the left pulvinar-amygdala connection.
source: We observed hemispheric lateralisation of the pulvinar-amygdala connection, such that both the local and global tractography showed greater fibre density along the right than the left, and there were stronger tractography-behaviour and tractography-connectivity relationships for the right than the left.
evidence: Summary of lateralization findings from correlation analyses

claim: Early studies on the subcortical route observed specifically right-sided BOLD responses during non-conscious fearful face viewing.
source: Early studies on the subcortical route observed specifically right-sided BOLD responses during non-conscious fearful face viewing (Morris et al., 1999; Morris et al., 1998), and a previous tractography study has also found that only the fractional anisotropy of the right subcortical route was significantly related to threat-biased saccades (Koller et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Morris et al., 1999; Morris et al., 1998; Koller et al., 2018

claim: Only the fractional anisotropy of the right subcortical route was significantly related to threat-biased saccades.
source: Early studies on the subcortical route observed specifically right-sided BOLD responses during non-conscious fearful face viewing (Morris et al., 1999; Morris et al., 1998), and a previous tractography study has also found that only the fractional anisotropy of the right subcortical route was significantly related to threat-biased saccades (Koller et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koller et al., 2018

claim: There is mounting evidence for right-sided specialisation for ordered and disordered emotion processing.
source: There is mounting evidence for right-sided specialisation for ordered (Wyczesany et al., 2018) and disordered (McDonald, 2017) emotion processing, particularly for non-conscious signals transmitted along the subcortical route (Gainotti, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wyczesany et al., 2018; McDonald, 2017; Gainotti, 2012

claim: Local tractography covaried with fearful face recognition scores while global tractography covaried with effective connectivity.
source: One limitation of the present study is the discrepancy between how local and global measures of fibre density related to other measures; namely, that local tractography covaried with fearful face recognition scores while global tractography covaried with effective connectivity.
evidence: Summary of discrepancy in findings between methods

claim: It is possible that the local tractography's relatively greater susceptibility to noise may have decreased its relationship to corresponding effective connectivity parameters.
source: While the reconstructed fibres shared many similarities (e.g. the pattern of findings for each connection across hemispheres and subregions, as well as the overlap with major fasciculi; see Figure 1) even after accounting for head motion, it is possible that the local tractography's relatively greater susceptibility to noise may have decreased its relationship to corresponding effective connectivity parameters.
evidence: Speculation about methodological limitation with reference to Figure 1

claim: Global tractography has been shown to better reflect local connection architecture.
source: Indeed, global tractography has been shown to better reflect local connection architecture (Jbabdi and Johansen-Berg, 2011), such as the subcortical connections we have investigated.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jbabdi and Johansen-Berg, 2011

claim: Discrepancies between global and local tractography have been reported in other work.
source: Such discrepancies between global and local tractography have been reported in other work (Anastasopoulos et al., 2014) and so further research (particularly those that only recruit a single tractograpy method) will benefit from specific investigations into why these discrepancies might arise.
evidence: Supported by citation to Anastasopoulos et al., 2014

claim: The multimodal neuroimaging approach provides convergent evidence for a fundamental and conserved pulvinar-amygdala pathway that is specifically involved in fear.
source: In conclusion, our study has made substantial progress towards settling the long-held debate over the existence and function of a subcortical route to the amygdala in the human brain. Our multimodal neuroimaging approach, leveraged by computational modelling, provides convergent evidence for a fundamental and conserved pulvinar-amygdala pathway that is specifically involved in fear.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from all study findings

claim: The white matter tracts that form the subcortical structural pathway from the pulvinar to the amygdala enable functional, dynamic interactions involved in emotional face perception.
source: We demonstrate that the white matter tracts that form the subcortical structural pathway from the pulvinar to the amygdala enables functional, dynamic interactions involved in emotional face perception.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from correlation between structural and functional measures

claim: Structural connectivity between the pulvinar and the amygdala leads to better recognition of fearful expressions.
source: Critically, we show that structural connectivity between the pulvinar and the amygdala leads to better recognition of fearful expressions.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from correlation between structural measures and behavior

claim: The final sample consisted of 622 participants aged between 22 and 36 years (M = 28.81, SD = 3.68 years), 259 of whom were male and 363 female.
source: This resulted in a final sample of 622 participants aged between 22 and 36 years (M = 28.81, SD = 3.68 years), 259 of whom were male and 363 female, with 569 right-handed and 53 left-handed.
evidence: Description of sample demographics

claim: Within the sample, 495 participants were related to one or more other participants (328 families in total).
source: Within our sample, 495 participants were related to one or more other participants (328 families in total). This included 53 pairs of monozygotic twins, 50 pairs of dizygotic twins, and 289 participants with one or more non-twin siblings in the sample.
evidence: Description of sample composition

claim: Global tractography is a Bayesian approach to reconstructing whole-brain fibre configurations that best explain DWI data.
source: Global tractography is a data-driven Bayesian approach to estimating the whole-brain fibre configuration that best explains the underlying diffusion-weighted images.
evidence: Description of methodological approach

claim: Global tractography accounts for the spatial continuity of fibres and thus is better able to discriminate crossing and fanning fibre geometries.
source: As opposed to local streamline tracking, global tractography accounts for the spatial continuity of fibres and thus is better able to discriminate crossing and fanning fibre geometries (Christiaens et al., 2015).
evidence: Description of methodological advantage supported by citation to Christiaens et al., 2015

claim: The density of the final tractogram quantitatively represents the apparent fibre density.
source: Furthermore, because the simultaneously-reconstructed fibre configurations are optimised with respect to the data at hand, the density of the final tractogram quantitatively represents the apparent fibre density (AFD; i.e. the proportion of space occupied by white matter fibres (Raffelt et al., 2012).
evidence: Description of methodological property supported by citation to Raffelt et al., 2012

claim: SIFT2 weights the streamlines by a cross-sectional multiplier such that the sum of these weighting factors better represents the underlying white matter fibre density.
source: SIFT2 makes this possible by weighting the streamlines by a cross-sectional multiplier such that the sum of these weighting factors better represents the underlying white matter fibre density (Smith et al., 2012).
evidence: Description of methodological approach supported by citation to Smith et al., 2012

claim: Dynamic Causal Modelling infers the causal direction of information flow between neural regions using a biophysically informed generative model.
source: We implemented Dynamic Causal Modelling (DCM) to infer the causal direction of information flow between neural regions using a biophysically informed generative model (Friston et al., 2003).
evidence: Description of methodological approach supported by citation to Friston et al., 2003

claim: 237 out of the 622 participants had above-threshold activation within each ROI across both scanning sessions.
source: To specify a DCM, each participant needed to have above-threshold activation (at p < 0.05, uncorrected) within each ROI across both scanning sessions. This was the case for 237 out of the 622 participants (see Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: Description of sample selection for DCM analysis

claim: The group of 237 participants with above-threshold BOLD responses in all ROIs did not differ significantly from the other group of 385 participants in the global or local tractography results.
source: Critically, the group of 237 participants with above-threshold BOLD responses in all ROIs did not differ significantly from the other group of 385 participants in the global or local tractography results (main effect of 'group' and interactions with 'group' were all p > 0.162 and ηp2 <.003), performance on the Penn Emotion Recognition task (all independent-samples t-tests had p > 0.100), volume of the thalamus (left: p = 0.055, right: p = 0.987)/amygdala (left: p = 0.472, right: p = 0.394)/fusiform area (left: p = 0.677, right: p = 0.597)/lateral occipital area (left: p = 0.762, right: p = 0.679; volumes computed by Freesurfer), median reaction time (faces: p = 0.418, shapes: p = 0.617) and accuracy (faces: p = 0.417, shapes: p = 0.717) during the fMRI task, age (p = 0.782), or gender (p = 0.359).
evidence: Result from statistical comparisons between subsamples

claim: There was no evidence to assume that the DCM sample was biased by any confounding variable.
source: Therefore, using the information available to us, we had no evidence to assume that our DCM sample was biased by any confounding variable.
evidence: Inference drawn from subsample comparison results
